title: Monotone Subsequence Bound Tightening
prompt:
Part 1 — PROOF:
Prove the Erdős–Szekeres theorem: every sequence of n² + 1 distinct real numbers contains a monotone (increasing or decreasing) subsequence of length at least n + 1.

Your proof must be fully rigorous. If you use a pigeonhole argument on labels (longest increasing subsequence length, longest decreasing subsequence length), you must:
1. Define the labelling precisely.
2. Prove that no two elements share the same label pair.
3. Complete the pigeonhole argument with explicit bounds.

Part 2 — TIGHT CONSTRUCTION:
For n = 4 (so n² + 1 = 17), construct an explicit sequence of 16 distinct real numbers (i.e., n² elements) such that the longest monotone subsequence has length exactly 4 (i.e., exactly n). This demonstrates the bound n² + 1 is tight.

Your construction must:
1. List all 16 numbers explicitly.
2. Prove that no increasing subsequence of length 5 exists.
3. Prove that no decreasing subsequence of length 5 exists.
4. Exhibit an increasing or decreasing subsequence of length exactly 4.

The standard construction arranges numbers in an n × n grid read in a specific order. If you use this approach, specify the grid, the reading order, and verify the claimed properties. Do not simply assert 'by construction' — demonstrate the properties hold for your specific sequence.
verification_method: Two-part audit: (1) The proof must be logically complete with no gaps. The pigeonhole argument must correctly show that if all increasing subsequences have length ≤ n and all decreasing subsequences have length ≤ n, then at most n² distinct labels exist, contradicting the sequence having n² + 1 elements. (2) The construction for n = 4 must be an explicit sequence of 16 numbers. Verify computationally that the longest increasing subsequence has length 4 and the longest decreasing subsequence has length 4. The standard tight example uses the sequence (n, n-1, ..., 1, 2n, 2n-1, ..., n+1, 3n, ..., 2n+1, ..., n², ..., n²-n+1) — i.e., n blocks of n elements, each block decreasing, blocks arranged so that picking one from each block gives an increasing subsequence.
why_frontier_hard: The proof itself is manageable, but the tight construction is where models fail. Common errors: (1) producing a sequence of the wrong length (17 instead of 16, or 15), (2) confusing row-major and column-major grid orderings and producing a sequence that actually contains a monotone subsequence of length 5, (3) claiming the construction works without verifying no length-5 monotone subsequence exists, (4) giving n = 3 examples instead of n = 4.
ground_truth_notes: The Erdős–Szekeres theorem is tight: for n² elements, one can avoid any monotone subsequence of length n + 1. Standard construction for n = 4: (4, 3, 2, 1, 8, 7, 6, 5, 12, 11, 10, 9, 16, 15, 14, 13). This has longest increasing subsequence length 4 (e.g., 4, 8, 12, 16) and longest decreasing subsequence length 4 (e.g., 4, 3, 2, 1). Any permutation of n blocks of n reverse-sorted consecutive integers works, provided blocks are arranged in increasing order of their elements.
